title: Seventh commandment (CCC 2401–2449)
hookLine: don't steal, pay fair wages, share the earth's goods

lines: A BORROWED LADDER IN THE GARAGE.
A TAX COLLECTOR IN A TREE.
cards: In the back of a garage, behind the bikes, leans a ladder. It belongs to the neighbor. It was borrowed for one gutter job, a few summers ago, and it has quietly become part of the furniture.
Nobody would call it stealing. Nobody would call it giving back, either.

In Jericho, a rich tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus pass, and before the day is over he's promising to pay back fourfold anyone he has cheated. The seventh commandment reaches from the ladder to the tax office.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not steal." Four words, and the Catechism builds a whole picture of economic life on them.
It starts with creation: God entrusted the earth and its resources to the common stewardship of humanity, and its goods are meant for the whole human race.
Private property is legitimate; it secures freedom and dignity and helps people meet their needs.
But owning something doesn't cancel that first purpose: what a person owns is held for their family and, in some way, for others too.
Then theft, widened. Not only taking what isn't yours, but keeping things lent or found. Fraud in business.
Unjust wages. Raising prices by exploiting someone's ignorance or hardship. Work done poorly.
Tax evasion. Waste. The ladder in the garage belongs on that list.
And it asks for repair: what was taken should be given back. That's Zacchaeus, whom you met up a tree in year one.
He tells Jesus he'll give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold to anyone he has wronged, and Jesus answers that salvation has come to that house.
A just wage, the Catechism says, is the legitimate fruit of work; withholding it can be a grave injustice.
And it ends with love for the poor, quoting Gregory the Great, in paraphrase: when we give the poor what they need, we aren't giving them what's ours, but returning what's theirs.
Theft, here, isn't only a hand in someone's pocket. It's anything that keeps the earth's goods from the people they were made for.

how: Catholics are taught to make restitution for what they've taken, to pay and work fairly, and to give to the poor through almsgiving, parish collections and the works of mercy.

o: a rule only against taking things by force
a ban on owning any private property at all
respect for goods, and sharing them with all

games.q: the seventh commandment — tap the pairs.
p: meant for the whole human race
giving the poor what is theirs

s: the seventh commandment is only about taking things
the Catechism also names keeping things lent, unjust wages, fraud, poor work and waste.
the Catechism calls it legitimate, while holding that the earth's goods are meant for all.
the Catechism asks for things taken to be given back
repair is part of the commandment, as Zacchaeus shows.

games.q: you're Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector. Jesus has just invited himself to your house, and the crowd is muttering. what do you do?
o: keep quiet and enjoy the dinner.
give half your goods to the poor, and repay anyone you cheated fourfold.
hand back the exact amount and no more.
games.why: in Luke 19, Zacchaeus stands and promises half to the poor and fourfold repayment, and Jesus says salvation has come to that house.

practice: Think through the people whose work you'll use today, the driver, the server, the cashier, the voice on the help line, and picture one of them clearly, on their long shift.
Decide what fair looks like for them, a better tip, a prompt payment, a real thank-you, and if anything borrowed is still in your house, when it goes back. If you pray, ask for a generous hand.

wordCard.voice: Seventh commandment. Thou shalt not steal: respect for others' goods, fair wages, honest work, repair of what was taken, and the earth's goods shared with all, especially the poor. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: goods are for all. Even the ladder in the garage can still go home. That's today.

sources.ref: Gregory the Great, Regula Pastoralis 3.21, quoted in CCC 2446
